name: Cacao use at Santa Ana-La Florida, upper Amazon
summary: A directly dated residue documents cacao use at Santa Ana-La Florida in southeast Ecuador about 5,300 years ago. Later funerary bottles at the site also contained cacao residues.
description: Charred residue on sherd PLD-005 attests to early cacao use at Santa Ana-La Florida in southeast Ecuador. Researchers identified cacao in separate funerary stirrup-spout bottles dating to contexts around 4,000 cal BP. The form of any preparation and the manner in which the plant was obtained remain uncertain.

impact.note: One society in one region used it (reach 1); a new food and drink plant added to an existing diet (depth 1); later cacao use elsewhere may descend from upper Amazon use, but no source here ties it to this community, so generativity stays at 1.

date.label: 5440–5310 cal BP (c. 3490–3360 BCE)
date.basis: Zarrillo et al. Table 1 gives the calibrated range for directly dated charred residue PLD-005, Beta-312078.

events.statement: In charred residue from ceramic sherd PLD-005, researchers identified Theobroma starch, theobromine and a DNA signal specific to T. cacao. They radiocarbon dated the bulk charred residue.

evidence.locator: p. 1881, Table 1, PLD-005 and note a, and Fig. 2d
evidence.supports: Gives the calibrated age of the bulk residue and distinguishes DNA capture evidence for T. cacao from starch identifiable as Theobroma.

events.caveats: The range applies to the residue on PLD-005. The cacao-positive stirrup-spout bottles came from later tomb contexts.

earliest_record.rationale: The charred residue PLD-005 gives the earliest directly dated cacao evidence described at this site.

unresolved.note: Coordinates of Santa Ana-La Florida: the place is given as the town of Palanda, the canton centre near the site, because no fetched source gave site coordinates.
Whether the upper Amazon people domesticated cacao or only gathered wild pods; the genomic domestication signal in Central America dates to about 3,600 years ago.
How and when cacao reached Mesoamerica, and whether Mesoamerican chocolate needs its own derived record.

Later analyses report cacao in regional ceramic assemblages assigned to phases that overlap or begin before the Santa Ana-La Florida date. Directly dated specimen contexts and finer genetic comparisons would help resolve priority and regional movement.

evidence.supports: Sampled San Jacinto and Valdivia items are assigned to broad cultural intervals. The study reports multiple genetic affinities in coastal assemblages.

unresolved.note: Cacao-positive residues in the later stirrup-spout bottles support an association with funerary offerings. The residues leave the recipe and use of fermentation open.

evidence.locator: pp. 1880–1882, Fig. 2, Table 1 and the DNA capture discussion
evidence.supports: PLD-001 and PLD-002 are positive bottles from tombs. The contextual date estimates are around 4,000 cal BP.
The excavation report discusses cacao residues in vessels in the context of funerary offerings.

research.note: Zarrillo et al. used several analytical methods on material from this site. The early sherd residue was dated directly. The two later bottles date to their tomb contexts. Site-to-site priority requires sample-level dating.
